prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I opened with topological insulators first and optical lattice clocks second, and I have moved optical lattice clocks to the top after reading the ballots. The prize is for a discovery or invention, and the committee has to identify the topic and the people responsible for the original work. Here that is unusually clean. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium clocks. Ye took the clocks to the 10^-18 regime and showed what the approach can do for stability and accuracy. The concept is original, the result is quantitative and reproduced by several independent laboratories and species, and it already underpins geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the pending redefinition of the second. Two names carry it with little left over. Of the candidates in the first rank of support, it is the only one where I do not have to choose between a defensible and a contested credit allocation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision spectroscopy and optical clocks have been recognised repeatedly (Hall and Haensch in 2005, Wineland in 2012), so the committee may see this as the continuation of a heavily honoured line. There is also a judgement about Ye's weight relative to other contributors and about the timing of the SI second redefinition. I treat the redefinition as an application milestone and not as a scientific doubt. The idea itself is distinct, because the many-atom lattice with Lamb-Dicke confinement is conceptually different from single-ion clocks. My second concern is that topological insulators are the field I rated highest on conceptual reach, and choosing clocks first may under-weight that.

responses.point: Mehlig put fluctuation theorems first and topological insulators second, and noted that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are hard to accommodate in a three-name topological-insulator prize.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution point and it is the main reason I have moved off topological insulators as my first choice. In my opening I preferred Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan but acknowledged that was a judgement from recollection. Reading Mehlig, I see that leaving out Mele, who co-authored the founding Kane-Mele work, makes the allocation harder to defend than I had allowed. I would still keep B018 as my first alternative. I am less persuaded by fluctuation theorems as the lead. Mehlig's own opening shows that the credit among Jarzynski, Crooks, Evans, Gallavotti and Cohen is unsettled, and no other member ranked it, which suggests the experimental and conceptual reach is not yet broadly established for this committee.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first and described Katori's magic-wavelength concept and Ye's demonstrations of record stability as redefining precision measurement, with Katori and Ye covering the core.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name allocation and find Lindroth's framing of many-atom averaging combined with Lamb-Dicke confinement the sharpest statement of why this is a new regime and not an incremental clock. The reservation I would add is that single-ion clocks are already honoured through Wineland in 2012 and Hall and Haensch in 2005. A citation should therefore stress the lattice concept and the 10^-18 performance, and should not describe optical clocks in general. Lindroth ranks B030 second and B018 third, which tracks my own view that the moire and topological fields are the strongest condensed-matter alternatives.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranked IceCube first and topological insulators second, but favoured the version that includes the quantum anomalous Hall effect with Xue (B003), and argued that the IceCube credit needs a judgement that lets two names represent a large instrument collaboration.
responses.response: I take the collaboration point seriously and it is why I keep B014 below clocks. The discovery of a diffuse astrophysical flux is solid, but crediting Halzen and Karle for a detector built and analysed by hundreds of people is a harder attribution than Katori and Ye. On B003 versus B018, I disagree with bundling the quantum anomalous Hall effect into the topological insulator prize. It is a separate experimental achievement in magnetically doped films, and adding Xue in place of Hasan removes the first three-dimensional topological insulator observation. If the committee wants a topological prize, I think B018 is the cleaner statement of one discovery, though neither version resolves the Mele question.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first as a clear, nameable discovery of nature opening a new window on the universe, and rated its maturity as good because the diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels.
responses.response: I agree this is a genuine discovery and that it fits the prize criteria well. Where I differ is on maturity and attribution. The diffuse flux is established, but the identification of individual sources is more recent and has limited confirmation from other detectors, and I am not convinced the committee can name Halzen and Karle without leaving out others who built the project. I would not oppose B014 as a later prize. I do not think it should displace a candidate where the credit and the independent confirmation are both clearer.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes for precision spectroscopy and single-ion control.
How to weigh Ye against other leading contributors to lattice-clock performance, since the credited set cannot include them.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should count as a reason to wait, which I do not believe it should.
For the topological alternative, how to treat Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal within three names, which I cannot settle from the supplied text.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I share an institution (Chalmers) with Goran Johansson, but no connection to any credited name on the shortlist is documented. My electron-microscopy work on interfaces and oxides is not directly tied to any of the credited candidates.
